name: French Eclectic

geography.hearth: the Philadelphia Main Line and the Long Island North Shore

lineage.note: The principal claimed ancestor - the small provincial manor house of the Ile-de-France, Touraine and Normandy.
Source of the flared eave, the segmental dormer, the stucco-over-rubble wall and the informal L-plan.
The half-timbered and round-towered Norman register; where this dominates the result is french-normandy-revival.
The formal symmetrical subtype, quoting Louis XV and Louis XVI town and country houses rather than farm buildings.
The real descent. Delano & Aldrich, Carrere & Hastings, Trumbauer, Mellor Meigs & Howe - Ecole-derived offices with French plate books on the shelf.
Informal planning, grouped fenestration and the deliberate cultivation of the picturesque came through the same Anglo-American channel that produced Tudor Revival.
Same offices, same buyers, same masonry-veneer economics; the two styles share a kit almost entirely and differ in roof geometry and ornament.

description.short: The interwar American reading of the French provincial manor and farmhouse, distinguished from its English-derived neighbours by a tall hipped roof of near-equal pitch on all sides, flared at the eave, and by dormers that break the cornice line.
description.long:
French Eclectic is the quietest of the big interwar revivals and the hardest to name from memory, because its identity rests almost entirely on roof geometry. Where Tudor Revival organises itself around gables and Colonial Revival around a symmetrical facade, French Eclectic organises itself around a steep hipped roof - 12:12 and up - that runs at the same pitch on all four sides, comes down low, and very often flares outward at the eave in the characteristic bell curve of a French provincial roof. Under that roof the house may be symmetrical or rambling, brick or stone or stucco, three bays or nine. The roof is what makes it French.

The style has an unusually specific catalyst: the First World War. Between 1917 and 1919 something over a million American soldiers spent extended periods in the villages of northern France, and a great many of the young architects and draughtsmen among them came home with sketchbooks. That experience arrived in offices already primed by Ecole training and by a well-established American taste for French academic classicism, and it converted French building from an aristocratic reference - the chateau, which only Vanderbilts could afford - into a domestic one. The 1920s house market was the beneficiary. Publishers ran plate books of Normandy farm buildings; Mellor, Meigs & Howe in Philadelphia and Delano & Aldrich in New York built the high end; and by 1930 the suburban builder could produce a passable French Eclectic in brick veneer with a steep hip and two segmental dormers.

What the buyer was claiming is worth stating precisely, because it differs from the Tudor claim. Tudor asserts ancestry - English descent, old family, inherited land. French asserts cultivation - taste acquired rather than inherited, travel, education, an eye. This is why French Eclectic appears disproportionately among clients who were self-consciously modern: it flattered people who wanted to be understood as sophisticated rather than as old. It is also why the style tolerates so much variety. A house that claims taste can be symmetrical or informal without contradiction, whereas a house that claims lineage must be consistent.

In front of one, the roof does the work. It is large - often more than half the visible height of the building - and because the pitch is constant on every face, the building reads as a solid under a lid rather than as a set of gables. The flare at the eave softens the meeting of roof and wall and casts a long, low shadow, and the eye follows that line all the way round the house. Dormers push up through it, arched or segmental, with their own little hipped or eyebrow roofs. The wall below is usually calm: stucco or brick with quoins, tall casements often running to the floor, shutters that in the best examples actually work. The entrance is modest, sometimes only a stone surround and an arched door. The whole composition is less theatrical than Tudor and less insistent than Colonial, and it ages better than either.

defining_characteristics: Steeply pitched hipped roof, 12:12 or steeper, at substantially the same pitch on all faces, with the ridge short relative to the plan
Eave carried low and, in most examples, flared outward in a bell curve over the wall head
Dormers that break through the cornice line, most often arched or segmental-headed with hipped or eyebrow roofs
Massive masonry or stucco wall with quoins, water table, or other expression of thickness at reveals and corners
Tall casement windows, frequently paired and running near to the floor, with true divided lights and functional shutters
Absence of a dominant front-facing gable - the element that would immediately make the house read as English
diagnostic_tells: Hipped roof of equal pitch on all four sides with no front gable. One dominant cross-gable and the house is Tudor Revival, not French Eclectic.
The eave flare: a change of rafter angle in the bottom 18-30 in. of the roof, producing a visible upward curve. Nothing English does this.
Dormers cut through the wall head so that their cheeks are masonry continuous with the wall below, rather than sitting entirely on the roof slope.
Windows are casements, not double-hung, and their proportion is tall - 1:2.5 or better - with the head often segmental or round.
Chimneys are tall, slim and often stuccoed, placed at ridge ends; the massive corbelled brick stack of Tudor Revival is absent.

distinguished_from.difference: Chateauesque is aristocratic, load-bearing cut stone, and vertical, with turrets, cresting and late Gothic ornament on a Loire chateau model. French Eclectic is domestic, usually veneered or stuccoed, and takes the small manor and the farmhouse as its models, with almost no carved ornament.

Roof geometry decides it. Tudor Revival is gabled, English-referenced, and depends on half-timbering and a massive chimney; French Eclectic is hipped, French-referenced, flares its eave, and uses casements without applied timbering.

The original is a masonry building of two-foot walls with a plan generated by defensible parti and generations of accretion, small windows and interior circulation through rooms. The revival is a single-campaign house with a corridor plan, large glazing, and a roof that is imitated rather than framed to carry slate or thatch.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof-dominant. The hipped roof mass is designed first and the wall is sized to sit beneath it; wall thickness expression at reveals and quoins sets the secondary scale. No classical module except in the formal symmetrical subtype, where a nominal French order governs the entrance.
typical_ratios: Roof height eave to ridge 0.6 to 1.0 times wall height, so the roof reads as 40-50 percent of the elevation
Roof pitch 12:12 to 18:12, constant within 1:12 on all faces
Eave flare: rafter angle reduced by 15-25 degrees over the bottom 18-30 in. of slope
Casement leaf 18-24 in. wide by 54-84 in. high; paired openings 1:2.5 to 1:3 overall
Wall reveal at openings 5-8 in. in masonry examples
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even and calm in the symmetrical subtype - three, five or seven bays with a centred entrance - and loosely grouped in the informal subtype, where wings of differing height meet at right angles and each carries its own regular fenestration.

massing_affinities.note: The informal subtype: an L or a T of hipped volumes at differing heights, often with a round entrance tower at the junction.
The formal symmetrical subtype - a double-pile block with a centred entrance under a tall hip.
Estate examples with projecting wings enclosing a forecourt.
Where service ranges and stabling are pulled into the composition, as in a Norman farm court.
A dominant front-facing gable converts the house to Tudor Revival.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch not less than 12:12 and constant within 1:12 across all faces. No front-facing gable may occupy more than 25 percent of the primary elevation width; a dominant front gable voids the style.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch floor. 'Constant within 1:12 across all faces' and the front-gable-width cap (<=25% of primary elevation width, no matching vocabulary variable) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Dormers of the principal rank must be wall dormers whose cheeks continue the wall material and whose sills sit at or below the eave line. Roof-set dormers set entirely above the eave are permitted only as secondary attic lights.

Where an eave flare is used, the flare shall extend 18-30 in. up the slope with a rafter-angle reduction of 15-25 degrees, and shall be carried continuously around all hips. A flare on the front elevation only is forbidden.

Masonry or stucco walls must express thickness: minimum 5 in. reveal at window and door jambs, with quoins, water table, or a returned surround. Flush-set windows in a thin veneer wall read as builder-grade and break the style.

test.note: The quoins/water-table/returned-surround alternatives are categorical with no set threshold stated and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Windows shall be casements with true divided lights, minimum leaf proportion 1:2.5. Where shutters are used they must be board-and-batten or louvred, sized to cover the full opening, and hung on strap hinges with tiebacks.

test.note: Tests the minimum casement-leaf height:width proportion (reusing the corpus's general opening-proportion variable for a casement leaf rather than a double-hung sash). Shutter material and hardware (board-and-batten or louvred, strap hinges, tiebacks) stay prose.

exemplars.name: Oheka Castle
exemplars.note: Delano & Aldrich for Otto Kahn; begun 1914. French chateau parti executed in fireproof steel and concrete - the grand end from which the suburban version is reduced.

exemplars.name: Nemours
exemplars.note: Carrere & Hastings for Alfred I. du Pont, in the Louis XVI manner with gardens after the Petit Trianon. Precedes the suburban floruit and defines its formal subtype.

exemplars.name: The Elms
exemplars.note: Horace Trumbauer, after the Chateau d'Asnieres. Included as the academic French model that the interwar suburban style domesticates.

exemplars.name: French Village
exemplars.location: Chestnut Hill / Mount Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: Robert Rodes McGoodwin, 1925-1928. A whole development of French provincial houses; the point at which the style becomes a suburban product. See also french-normandy-revival.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)
Robert A. M. Stern, Gregory Gilmartin and Thomas Mellins, New York 1930 (1987)
John Milnes Baker, American House Styles: A Concise Guide (1994)

proportion_packs.note: The twentieth-century American reading of the manoir, and the node most likely to be asked for by a real brief. It had no module or system pack at all before this -- `facade-picturesque` and two optionals -- so the elevation had nothing saying where a dormer goes. That is the failure this pack is for: French Eclectic dormers get placed by what the attic plan wants, and the dormer/count rule (exactly one per travee, on the bay's axis) is the corrective, stated as a single value because there is no second correct answer.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The style's own proportional_system calls itself 'roof-dominant' with 'no classical module except in the formal symmetrical subtype', which is exactly the picturesque system's governing logic - a dominant mass (here, the hipped roof itself rather than a gable) that every other element is subordinate to. Applies across both the symmetrical and informal subtypes described in massing_affinities; even the 'near-symmetrical' formal subtype is a calm massed composition rather than a bay-rhythm classical front, and facade-classical's own applies_to list does not extend to this node.

JUDGMENT BINDING, held at low precedence and marked optional deliberately. The style's own proportional_system states 'a nominal French order governs the entrance' in the formal symmetrical subtype only - Nemours and the Louis XVI-derived estate end of the style. No order-system pack's applies_to names french-eclectic, so this is general typological reasoning rather than a documented fit: Ionic is chosen over Corinthian or Composite because the style's own description insists the entrance stays modest ('sometimes only a stone surround and an arched door'), and Ionic is the order the corpus elsewhere treats as the restrained, non-triumphal choice. Do not apply to the informal subtype, which the style explicitly describes as having 'almost no carved ornament'.

JUDGMENT BINDING for the formal symmetrical subtype only, paired with the order accent above. The lineage record gives this style a direct, weight-1.0 descent from beaux-arts-american ('Delano & Aldrich, Carrere & Hastings, Trumbauer, Mellor Meigs & Howe - Ecole-derived offices with French plate books on the shelf'), which is the strongest lineage weight in the whole node and stronger than the arts-and-crafts-british edge (weight 0.5) that would argue for trim-craftsman instead. Deliberately not bound as primary or as the sole trim pack: the informal subtype, hybridized with tudor-revival (weight 0.6) and descended from arts-and-crafts-british, plausibly wants trim-craftsman, and asserting one trim family as THE answer for a style with two named subtypes would overstate what the sources settle. Both are left at 'optional' rather than one being forced to 'interior'.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes present Vignola's Composite as the most ornate of the five orders and are at pains to fix its identity in carved matter -- four diagonal volutes, two rows of acanthus, a denticular cornice with the large Composite dentil. This node's record names that order and refuses it in one clause, and the refusal is on exactly the slot the pack has taken: the cascade has Composite governing door_surround, which is the entrance the sentence is about. The record backs it a second time in distinguished_from chateauesque, where French Eclectic 'takes the small manor and the farmhouse as its models, with almost no carved ornament'. The node has bound vignola-ionic itself for the formal subtype's entrance; the Beaux-Arts ancestor's Composite is overriding that choice from two steps up.
declined_packs.quote: Ionic is chosen over Corinthian or Composite because the style's own description insists the entrance stays modest
declined_packs.note: Measured --impact: governs 2 slots, door_surround and frieze; both pass to palladio-tuscan (italian-renaissance). 0 slots lose all dimensioning. Measured with this pack declined alone; vignola-corinthian does not pick either slot up even when Composite is removed, which is consistent with its governing 0 slots today.
